name: Radicle
summary: A peer-to-peer code forge built on Git: every user runs a node that stores and shares repositories, and issues, patches and reviews travel inside the repository as signed Git objects, with no central server.
intro: In Radicle every participant runs a node, identified by an Ed25519 public key, its Node ID. `rad init` turns an ordinary Git repository into a Radicle one with a Repository ID such as `rad:z3gqc…`, derived from the hash of its first identity document: a small JSON file, kept at `refs/rad/id`, that lists the project’s name, default branch, its delegates (the people or bots who maintain it) and how many of them must agree. Nodes gossip three kinds of signed messages, about which nodes exist, which repositories each one holds and when references change, and move the data itself with Git’s own fetch protocol. A repository stays available as long as at least one node that seeds it is online, and anyone can run an always-on seed node.

No server decides what is true. Each peer’s branches live in a namespace named after its Node ID, all sharing one Git object store, and every node signs its references whenever they change. The canonical default branch is whatever enough delegates have pushed: with a threshold of two of three, a commit becomes canonical once two delegates have it. Issues and patches are collaborative objects, Git commit graphs inside the repository that peers merge by union and replay in a fixed order, so they work offline and sync like code. `git push rad HEAD:refs/patches` opens a patch.

The Heartwood stack is written in Rust, licensed under MIT and Apache 2.0, and funded by grants from Radworks; it does not use a blockchain or token. Radicle 1.0 shipped in September 2024, the latest release is 1.10.3 (September 8, 2026), and in April 2026 the project moved to radicle.dev and radicle.network. On September 23, 2026 it disclosed that traffic between nodes has never been encrypted or properly authenticated, so private repositories can leak to anyone on the network path; the fix, moving to the iroh networking stack, will be a breaking change.
strengths: No single host to trust or lose: any node can serve a repository, and signed references let anyone check updates without a central authority
Issues, patches and code review are stored in the repository, so they work offline and move with every clone
Plain Git underneath: you push to a `rad` remote, and tools that sit on Git, such as Jujutsu, keep working
Free software with no paid tier, platform account or cryptocurrency involved
limits: A repository is only reachable while some node seeding it is online, and the network is small: about 40 seed nodes at the 1.0 launch
Private repositories are unsafe over the network until the breaking protocol upgrade: as of October 2026 the project tells users to block them or stop their node
CI isn’t part of the core; in 2025 the team itself pushed branches to GitHub by hand to run tests with GitHub Actions
The planned move to iroh will split the network into upgraded and non-upgraded nodes that can’t talk to each other

snippet.title: Publish a repository and open a patch
source: rad auth                           # create your key pair (your Node ID) and alias
rad init                           # publish the current Git repository; it gets a rad: ID
rad node start                     # run your node in the background
git push rad HEAD:refs/patches     # open a patch; pushing again adds a revision
rad clone rad:z3gqcJUoA1n9HaHKufZs5FCSGazv5   # clone Radicle itself by its Repository ID
rad issue open                     # issues live in the repository too

story: Radicle began with Monadic, a Berlin company that Eleftherios Diakomichalis and Alexis Sellier (cloudhead) founded in January 2018 to build a “sovereign” developer stack: one that doesn’t depend on a large platform. The first Radicle, released as an alpha in February 2019, was built on IPFS.

Work on a second protocol, Radicle Link, began in October 2019. It drew on Secure Scuttlebutt and used Git itself for replication, dropping IPFS, and the Radicle Upstream desktop app shipped on it in December 2020. A Swiss non-profit, the Radicle Foundation, was set up in June 2020 to oversee the project, and from 2021 development was funded by Radworks.

In July 2022 the team started over again with Heartwood, the third-generation protocol, and discontinued Upstream. From January 2023 Radicle was developed on Radicle. After 17 release candidates, 1.0 shipped on September 10, 2024 with issues, patches, code review, private repositories and Tor support. In 2025 some ISPs blocked radicle.xyz, which the team blamed on content shown by its public repository explorer, so in April 2026 it split its site (radicle.dev) from the explorer (radicle.network).

choices.choice: Peer-to-peer instead of central or federated servers
choices.why: The goal is a forge with no single entity controlling the network or users’ data. In the 1.0 announcement the team wrote that sovereign code forges are “possible today, and in our opinion, necessary”, so free software doesn’t depend on large tech platforms.

IPFS was dropped after the first version. Since Radicle Link, repositories are ordinary bare Git repositories and peers fetch with Git’s own protocol, so existing Git tools keep working and each object is stored once.

choices.choice: Issues and patches as Git objects
choices.why: Storing collaborative objects as commit graphs in the repository means the social side of a project is replicated, verified and available offline exactly like the code, with no database to host.

choices.choice: Trust from signatures, not from a host
choices.why: Every node signs its references and a repository’s delegates decide its canonical branch, so anyone holding the Repository ID can verify an update without asking a trusted third party.

timeline.text: First Radicle alpha, on IPFS (February); work on Radicle Link begins (October)
Radicle Foundation set up (June); Upstream desktop app ships on Radicle Link (December)
Work starts on Heartwood, the third protocol (July)
Move to radicle.dev (April 23); 1.10.0 (August 5); network protocol vulnerability disclosed (September 23)
